source: Kyllonen & Christal (1990) Reasoning ability is (little more than) working-memory capacity?!
finding: Founding study. Four samples of US Air Force recruits. Latent working memory factor and latent reasoning factor correlated .80 to .90. Authors said reasoning is little more than WM capacity. Details here come from later papers, not the original.
numbers: 4 samples, N = 723, 412, 415, 594 (from a web search summary). 15 reasoning tests, 6 WM tasks (per Hagemann 2023). Latent r = .80 to .90.
limits: Original paper not opened (paywalled). WM tasks were chosen from a broad, vague definition; the authors admitted this was arbitrary.
agent_relevance: The strongest claim in the field: capacity is the core of reasoning. It is the origin of the idea of a limit on holding many rules.

source: Conway, Kane, Engle (2003) Working memory capacity and its relation to general intelligence
finding: Review of latent-variable studies. WM capacity and g are highly related but not the same. Kyllonen and Christal chose a varied-content, varied-process task battery because no task theory existed. Later work finds the link runs through executive attention under interference.
numbers: K&C latent r = .80 to .90. Ackerman et al 2002: r = .58 (WM-g). Conway et al 2002: r = .60. Conclusion: WM capacity accounts for at least one-third and perhaps one-half of the variance in g.
quote: WMC accounts for at least one-third and perhaps as much as one-half of the variance in g.
limits: Review, not new data. Restricted to latent-variable studies. The n-back link to WM span was untested at the time.
agent_relevance: Capacity alone is not the story. Control under interference is. For an agent: a long context is not the limit; managing competing items is.

source: Conway, Kane, Engle (2003) Working memory capacity and its relation to general intelligence (boundary condition: simple vs complex span)
finding: Complex span tasks (storage plus processing, e.g. operation span) load a different factor from simple span (digit span, word span). Complex span predicts g. Simple span does not. Complex span tasks correlate with each other only moderately.
numbers: Complex span tasks: Cronbach alpha .70 to .80; intercorrelations r = .40 to .60. Null correlation between simple span and g, found by Engle 1999 and replicated by Conway 2002.
limits: Based on a few latent-variable projects with student samples.
agent_relevance: Storing is not the predictive part. Holding while processing is. Tests of an agent should add a processing load while it holds items.

source: Conway, Kane, Engle (2003) Working memory capacity and its relation to general intelligence (executive attention account)
finding: High-span people beat low-span people only where interference or response competition exists. Example: a Sternberg scan variant with overlapping letter sets. The RT slope on set size was steeper for low WMC only when each letter belonged to two sets. No group difference with no overlap.
numbers: Overlap condition: low WMC slope steeper. No-overlap condition: slopes did not differ at all. High WMC: slopes equal in overlap and no-overlap.
limits: Median-split design; the review notes that splitting a continuous variable is not ideal.
agent_relevance: Add look-alike items and capacity limits appear; keep items distinct and they vanish. Supports guarding against interference.

source: Colom, Rubio, Shih, Santacreu (2006) Fluid intelligence, working memory and executive functioning
finding: Review of coefficients plus an own test of the executive account. The variance shared by WM and executive functioning did not explain the WM-intelligence link. Cites latent coefficients from .70 to .96 across studies.
numbers: N = 229 air traffic control applicants. WM-intelligence r = .20 (.27 corrected). WM-executive (Tower of Hanoi) r = -.20 (-.24 corrected). Cited coefficients: K&C .80-.88; Colom 2003 .70; Ackerman 2002 .70; Colom 2004 mean .96 (three large studies); Colom & Shih 2004 .86; Colom 2005 .89.
limits: One dual-task WM measure and one reasoning test; low raw r. Executive measure was Tower of Hanoi only.
agent_relevance: The link is not simply 'executive control'. Do not assume one mechanism.

source: Colom, Rubio, Shih, Santacreu (2006) Fluid intelligence, working memory and executive functioning (raw vs latent correlations)
finding: Latent-variable correlations are far above raw correlations. The Ackerman et al 2005 meta-analysis found a much lower mean correlation than K&C. Raw correlations of one WM task with Raven are small.
numbers: Raw r = .24 (Raven vs computation span, Ackerman 2002); r = .32 (Raven vs mental counters, Colom 2004). Meta-analytic WM-intelligence r = .36 as quoted here.
limits: The .36 figure is as quoted in this source; Hagemann 2023 quotes .48 for the same meta-analysis (see a09).
agent_relevance: A single WM score predicts only a small share of reasoning. Latent figures pool several tasks.

source: Colom, Rubio, Shih, Santacreu (2006) Fluid intelligence, working memory and executive functioning (Engle 1999, Miyake 2000-2001, Oberauer 2004 cited numbers)
finding: Executive-function measures correlate weakly with WM span. Dual-task cost, an executive measure, correlates .15 with a complex WM score. Oberauer 2004 concluded this rejects theories that equate WM with control of two tasks.
numbers: Engle 1999: random number generation vs WM span r = .14 to .18; vs Raven/CFT r = .05, .06; WM vs intelligence r = .24 to .34. Miyake 2000: operation span vs Tower of Hanoi .04, vs random number generation .17. Oberauer 2004: mean r = .15 (range .01 to .33).
limits: Figures are second-hand through Colom 2006.
agent_relevance: Splitting 'executive control' into parts shows weak links; do not design one all-purpose controller step.

source: Hagemann et al. (2023) Fluid Intelligence Is (Much) More than Working Memory Capacity: An Experimental Analysis
finding: Reviews the founding studies. K&C: four samples, 15 reasoning tests, 6 WM tasks, latent r = .80 to .90. Critique: reasoning and WM tests shared arithmetic content, so the r may partly reflect arithmetic skill.
numbers: Latent r = .80 to .90. Content overlap: arithmetic reasoning test in all four samples; mental arithmetic in samples 1, 2, 4; numerical assignment in samples 1, 2, 3.
limits: Overlap critique is argued, not tested here. K&C themselves said cause could run either way.
agent_relevance: Overlap of task content inflates links. When testing an agent, do not measure 'capacity' with the same skill used for reasoning.

source: Hagemann et al. (2023) Fluid Intelligence Is (Much) More than Working Memory Capacity: An Experimental Analysis (meta-analyses)
finding: Three summaries of WM-Gf size. Ackerman et al 2005: 86 samples, mean r = .48. Kane et al 2005: 14 data sets on fluid reasoning with latent models, r = .72. Oberauer et al 2005 reanalysis: r = .85. The field settles near 50 to 60 percent shared variance at latent level.
numbers: Ackerman: 86 samples, r = .48, CI .44 to .52. Kane: 14 data sets, r = .72, range .41 to 1.00. Oberauer: r = .85. Engle 1999: latent r = .59 (operation, reading, counting span; Raven SPM and Cattell CFT).
limits: Methods differ: Ackerman pooled many tasks; Kane kept latent studies only. The disagreement is about method.
agent_relevance: Quote a range, not one number. Capacity explains about half of reasoning variance in people.

source: Engle, Tuholski, Laughlin, Conway (1999) Working memory, short-term memory, and general fluid intelligence: a latent-variable approach
finding: Latent factor of WM span predicted Gf. A short-term memory factor did not add once WM was held. Conclusion: central executive or controlled attention drives the link.
numbers: Latent r = .59 (per Hagemann 2023). WM vs Raven/CFT raw r = .24 to .34 (per Colom 2006).
limits: Not opened; numbers second-hand from a06 and a09.
agent_relevance: Holding is not enough; control matters. Simple recall does not predict reasoning.

source: Ackerman, Beier, Boyle (2005) Working memory and intelligence: the same or different constructs?
finding: Meta-analysis claiming WM and intelligence are related but distinct. Mean r far below unity.
numbers: 86 samples, mean r = .48 (CI .44 to .52) per Hagemann 2023; .36 per Colom 2006.
limits: Not opened. Contested by Kane 2005 and Oberauer 2005 on methods (latent vs observed, content overlap).
agent_relevance: Do not treat WM and Gf as one thing.

source: Carpenter, Just, Shell (1990) What one intelligence test measures: a theoretical account of the processing in the Raven Progressive Matrices Test
finding: Production-system models of Raven: FAIRAVEN and BETTERAVEN. Both find correspondences, hold rules in a working memory buffer, then generate the missing cell. Difficulty rises with the number of rule tokens and the demand for goal management; BETTERAVEN adds goal management and abstraction.
numbers: Number of rule tokens explained 57% of variance in item accuracy (per Little 2014). XOR (distribution of 2) rules appear only at the end of the test where accuracy is lowest.
limits: Not opened; described through Little, Lewandowsky, Craig (2014). Some later item-wise studies did not see the predicted rise of WM load with difficulty (see a13).
agent_relevance: This is the 'limits on holding many rules' model. More rules to hold at once means more failure. An agent should count rules and split problems.

source: Little, Lewandowsky, Craig (2014) Working memory capacity and fluid abilities: the more difficult the item, the more more is better
finding: Earlier studies found the WM-Raven link flat across item difficulty, which seemed to reject Carpenter 1990. Simulation shows flatness appears only when the overall correlation is low. With a better composite WM measure, the item-wise link rises with difficulty.
numbers: Simulation: population r = .10, .30, .50, .70, .80, .90; 10,000 replications each. Study with 130 volunteers (N = 126 in final analysis), four WM tasks. Wiley et al 2011 had found invariance across 36 RAPM items.
quote: invariance can only be observed if the overall correlation between Raven's and WMC is low
limits: Item position is only a proxy for difficulty. Two studies, student samples, one country.
agent_relevance: Repairs the rule-holding account: the failed replications used weak WM measures. Supports testing an agent with rising rule count.

source: Chuderski (2013) When are fluid intelligence and working memory isomorphic and when are they not?
finding: Time pressure raises the WM-Gf link. Under heavy speeding the two are close to isomorphic; unspeeded, WM explains about a third to 38 percent.
numbers: Per a Scientific American blog summary (opened): review of 26 studies; study 1 N = 1,377 aged 15 to 46; speeded group 20 min, unspeeded group 60 min; WM explained 38% of variance in unspeeded group; about one third in study 2 without time pressure.
limits: Paper behind a paywall; not opened. Numbers come from a blog summary.
agent_relevance: Time limits inflate the capacity link. An agent under a tight budget will look more capacity-bound than one with room to think.

source: Hagemann et al. (2023) Fluid Intelligence Is (Much) More than Working Memory Capacity: An Experimental Analysis (Study 1 and Study 2: causal test)
finding: Experimental test: load working memory while solving Raven items. Study 1: four secondary tasks loaded the central executive, loop or sketchpad during APM items. Executive load cut APM scores. The effect was modest compared with the effect on span tasks in Study 2.
numbers: Study 1: N = 60 (13 male, 47 female; mean age 22.45). Task effect F(3,56) = 4.07, p = .011, eta squared = .13 (abstract: 15% of variance). Study 2: same load on complex span tasks explained 32, 36 and 48 percent (about 40%). Groups equal at baseline: WM F(3,56) = 1.42, Gf F(3,56) = 0.90. Study 1 vs 2 interaction F(3,111) = 3.11, p = .029, eta squared = .05.
quote: Fluid intelligence is (much) more than working memory capacity
limits: Small N, between-subject, students. A weaker effect on Raven than on span suggests WM is part of Gf, not all of it.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that load on the controller lowers reasoning, but only by 13 to 15 percent of variance. Reasoning has parts beyond holding.

source: Hagemann et al. (2023) Fluid Intelligence Is (Much) More than Working Memory Capacity: An Experimental Analysis (training studies cited)
finding: Describes the WM-training route to causation. Jaeggi 2008 reported Gf gains after dual n-back training. Chooi & Thompson 2012 and Redick 2013 did not replicate it with controls. The Scientific American summary of Chuderski adds that gains showed only under extreme time limits.
numbers: Redick 2013: placebo-controlled dual n-back training; experimental group improved on the trained task. No Gf transfer is reported in the text read.
limits: Only described; covered in the separate training subfield.
agent_relevance: Negative result: raising capacity by training does not reliably raise reasoning. No training shortcut.

source: Draheim, Pak, Draheim, Engle (2022) The role of attention control in complex real-world tasks
finding: Competing explanation: attention control explains the WM-Gf link. In a large latent study (Draheim 2021) the WM-Gf path was no longer significant once attention control was added. Full mediation appeared only with reliable, accuracy-based control tasks.
numbers: Draheim 2021: N = 396 students and community members; each construct measured by three tasks. Antisaccade and selective visual arrays had about five times, and modified Stroop and flanker about three times, the reliable variance of traditional Stroop and flanker. Adding RT-based tasks removed full mediation.
limits: Single dataset for the headline mediation; authors' own lab. Reliability of attention tasks is a general weakness (Hedge, Rey-Mermet, Rouder cited).
agent_relevance: Capacity may be the wrong frame. The agent needs a controller that keeps goals against interference.

source: Cochrane, Simmering, Green (2019) Fluid intelligence is related to capacity in memory as well as attention
finding: Reverses the attention-first order. N-back and spatial span (WM) and multiple object tracking and enumeration (attention) related to Raven. The attention-intelligence links were fully mediated by WM scores. Attention did not mediate WM-intelligence. Same pattern in children and adults.
numbers: Final sample 42 children plus adults; 2 children and 12 adults excluded for non-compliance. Raven's Progressive Matrices as Gf measure. Four tasks reliably linked to intelligence.
limits: Small sample. Authors expected no strong positive manifold.
agent_relevance: Competing finding to a17: the ordering of WM and attention is unsettled. Both capacity and control are needed.

source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2024) Working Memory Capacity of ChatGPT: An Empirical Study (AAAI)
finding: ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo) on verbal and spatial n-back. Performance falls as n goes 1 to 3; d' drops to about 1 at n = 3, like humans (human drop near n = 3). Noise symbols lower capacity. Chain-of-thought helps. GPT-4 has far larger capacity. Open 6-7B models have very low capacity.
numbers: Verbal variants (base, CoT, feedback): d' about 1 at n = 3. Larger spatial grids gave higher capacity (3x3 to 7x7). Abstract spatial reasoning variants lowered capacity. Models: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Vicuna-7B/13B, Bloomz-7B, ChatGLM-6B.
quote: ChatGPT has a working memory capacity limit strikingly similar to that of humans
limits: GPT-4 not tested above n = 3 (cost). Hu & Lewis 2025 show part of the drop is task misunderstanding.
agent_relevance: First test of a human WM paradigm on an LLM. A cheap probe of the same limit. The authors suggest capacity may index general ability.

source: Hu & Lewis (2025) Do Language Models Understand the Cognitive Tasks Given to Them? Investigations with the N-Back Paradigm
finding: Failed-replication style critique of Gong 2024. Poor 2- and 3-back is partly misunderstanding of the task: weak models give answers that fit an m-back with m not equal to n. The best model (Llama 3.1 70B) holds up to 10-back.
numbers: Retrieval accuracy at 1-, 2-, 3-back: Qwen1.5-14B 1.00/.09/.08; Llama3.1-8B 1.00/.14/.17; Gemma2-27B 1.00/.57/.36; GPT-3.5 1.00/.51/.43; Qwen2-72B 1.00/.81/.84; Llama3.1-70B 1.00/.99/.93. Llama 70B retrieval at n = 8, 9, 10: 75.25%, 66.08%, 57.1% (task accuracy 83.33%, 78.25%, 71.92%). With in-context curriculum demos: retrieval 79.83%, 80.17%, 71.67%; task accuracy 90.08%, 90.08%, 84.75%. 50 trials of 24 letters, 8 matches each.
quote: poor performance is due at least in part to a limitation in task comprehension and task set maintenance
limits: Open models only (Qwen, Llama, Gemma) plus GPT-3.5. Limits depend on instruction and demos, not a fixed number.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: the human 'capacity of about 3' does not carry over. Demos and curriculum raise it far. Check task understanding before inferring a limit.

source: Gong & Zhang (2024) Self-Attention Limits Working Memory Capacity of Transformer-Based Models
finding: Small decoder transformers trained from scratch on n-back lose accuracy as N rises. Attention to the N-back position grows during training. Total entropy of the attention matrix grows with N and is linked to the accuracy drop. Proposed cause: dispersed attention.
numbers: 1-layer 1-head model: Kruskal-Wallis H = 38.517, p < .001, eta squared = .248; logarithmic decline up to N = 6. Models with more layers or heads: over 95% accuracy at all N with slight declines. Sequence length 24.
limits: Toy models, not pretrained LLMs. Gong 2026 finds a second layer removes the constraint, so this is a limit of small models.
agent_relevance: A formal, mechanistic model of a capacity limit in an attention system. Suggests depth, not context length, sets the limit.

source: Liang, Zhu, Wang, Zhou (2026) Can Vision Replace Text in Working Memory? Spatial n-Back in Vision-Language Models
finding: Qwen2.5 vs Qwen2.5-VL on spatial n-back, text-rendered vs image-rendered grids. Text gives higher accuracy and d' than vision in all conditions. Nominal 2- and 3-back often follows a recency-locked comparison, not the instructed lag. Grid size changes interference.
numbers: Location recognition check on 200 random grids (Table 1); results by grid size for n = 1, 2, 3 (Fig 2). Exact d' values were not extracted.
limits: Small open models. Exact figures not captured.
agent_relevance: Representation matters: the same task as text vs image gives a different limit. Keep working state in text.

source: Gong (2026) Language Models Share a Readout Bottleneck in Working Memory
finding: 15 pretrained LLMs (70M to 14B parameters, three families) show falling d' as N rises and lure errors. Heads attend to the target on most missed matches. Linear probes still decode target vs lure near perfectly, even on false-alarm trials. Sharpening attention gains little; suppressing non-target letter content helps. The limit is reading out under interference, not finding the item.
numbers: Median d' 2.57 at N = 1 (range 1.25 to 4.28), 0.91 at N = 4, 0.52 at N = 6. Qwen2.5-14B: 4.28 at N = 1, 1.15 at N = 6. At N = 2, models say 'match' to 79% of N-1 lures vs 4% of other non-matches. Probe classifies 95% (N = 2) and 86% (N = 3) of lure false alarms as lures. Qwen2.5-14B half-strength suppression: d' 2.42 to 2.88, 1.60 to 3.38, 1.29 to 2.05 at N = 2, 3, 4. Head ablation cost less in larger models (Spearman 0.74, p = .002); suppression helped more (0.57, p = .03). Chat format Qwen2.5-Instruct 0.5B-7B: d' 1.8 to 2.0 at N = 1, 0.4 to 0.7 at N = 6.
limits: Letter N-back only. Single-author preprint. Sizes up to 14B. In minimal one-layer transformers precision does limit; a second layer removes it.
agent_relevance: Supports the human interference account. The scaffold should keep similar-looking items out of view together and filter them, rather than add context.

source: Xiong, Ji-An, Huang, Wilson, Lee, Wei (2026) In-context superposition: human-like working memory interference in LLMs (COLM)
finding: A two-layer transformer trained on N-back solves it perfectly, but ten trained LLMs show human-like limits, recency bias and lure effects. Memories sit in entangled form ('in-context superposition'); suppressing interference helps. Mean N-back accuracy correlates with MMLU Pro, GPQA Diamond and IFEval.
numbers: 10 models (Gemma3 1B-27B, Qwen3.5 2B-27B, Ministral3 14B, Llama3 8B). N-back accuracy vs benchmarks: Pearson r between .69 and .88 across six cells (autoregressive and teacher forcing; MMLU Pro .78/.70, GPQA .88/.72, IFEval .69/.82 as read from a garbled table, row assignment unclear). Log parameter count predicted none of the three. Lure and smaller-set-size effects correlated with accuracy (negative r about -.3 to -.5, table garbled).
quote: working memory capacity reflects the ability to select task-relevant information under interference
limits: Only 10 models, so correlations are fragile. Qwen3.5-27B exceeded the human curve while still declining with N.
agent_relevance: An LLM version of the K&C finding: capacity on a WM task tracks broader capability. N-back accuracy may be a cheap index of reasoning headroom.

source: Dokic, Koso-Drljevic, Bilalic (2025) Past reflections, present insights: a systematic review and new empirical research into the working memory - fluid intelligence relationship (Intelligence)
finding: Systematic review plus new data on WM and Gf. Only metadata found via Crossref; full text was paywalled and not read. No numbers are claimed.
numbers: No figures read.
limits: Not opened. ScienceDirect returned 403.
agent_relevance: Follow-up needed: likely the most recent summary of effect sizes and replication status.

source: Oberauer et al. (2018) benchmark and Colom et al. (2015) quasi-isomorphism (as cited in Hagemann 2023)
finding: Hagemann 2023 reports the field benchmark: WM capacity and Gf share about 50 to 60 percent of variance at the latent level, with r about .70 to .80 at most (Oberauer 2018).
numbers: Latent common variance 50 to 60 percent; r up to .70 to .80.
limits: Second-hand through Hagemann; original reviews not opened.
agent_relevance: Use 'about half' as the honest bound on how much capacity explains of reasoning.

source: Kyllonen & Christal 1990, limits of the headline (from Conway 2003 and Hagemann 2023)
finding: Both reviews flag the same limits of the founding study: arbitrary WM battery, overlapping arithmetic content between WM and reasoning tests, correlational design. The authors allowed a reverse causal reading.
numbers: Overlap: arithmetic reasoning in all four samples; mental arithmetic in 3 of 4; numerical assignment in 3 of 4. Later latent r fall to .58-.72 with other designs (Ackerman 2002 .58; Conway .60; Kane 2005 .72).
limits: No direct test of the overlap effect size in the sources read.
agent_relevance: The .80 to .90 headline is an upper bound. Plan for about half.

source: Replication picture of the LLM n-back result: Gong 2024 vs Hu & Lewis 2025 vs Gong 2026
finding: All later papers find accuracy falls with N across many models, so the pattern replicates. The explanation changed: task comprehension (Hu & Lewis), attention entropy in small models (Gong & Zhang), interference at readout (Gong 2026, Xiong 2026).
numbers: Gong 2026: all 15 models get worse as N grows; the k-back rule that best fits the answers differs from N in only 14 of 90 cases, all at N of 4 or more in small models.
limits: Different tasks (letters; chat vs completion format) limit comparison across papers.
agent_relevance: Do not claim 'LLMs have a capacity of 3'. Say: accuracy falls with load, and the cause is interference and instruction clarity.
